failure_modes.description: The assumption that intersections can calculate performance gradients is fundamentally flawed. Traffic systems are highly stochastic with numerous unmeasurable variables (driver behavior, weather, accidents) that make gradient calculation impossible in practice.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems exhibit chaotic behavior that cannot be modeled with deterministic gradients. Real-world traffic data shows high variance that cannot be reduced to simple gradient calculations.

failure_modes.description: The claim contradicts established knowledge in control theory and traffic engineering. Gradient descent requires smooth, convex optimization landscapes which traffic networks demonstrably do not possess.
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous studies have shown traffic networks are non-convex with multiple local optima, making gradient-based methods prone to failure. Existing successful systems use reinforcement learning or other non-gradient approaches.

failure_modes.description: The mechanism breaks down at network boundaries where intersections have fewer neighbors. The inverse proportionality to neighbor performance metrics would cause unstable behavior at perimeter intersections.
failure_modes.evidence: Any distributed system with boundary effects suffers from edge cases. The proposed mechanism would create different behavior patterns at network edges versus interior intersections, leading to systemic inefficiencies.

failure_modes.description: Similar approaches have been extensively researched and failed. The concept of distributed traffic signal optimization using gradient methods has been attempted multiple times with poor results.
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous papers from the 1990s-2000s attempted similar gradient-based approaches and abandoned them due to poor performance compared to other methods like reinforcement learning or model predictive control.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis is already falsified by its own expected failure modes. The predicted oscillations and convergence to local maxima are inherent flaws that cannot be resolved with the proposed mechanism.
failure_modes.evidence: The hypothesis explicitly predicts oscillatory behavior and suboptimal convergence - these are not edge cases but fundamental limitations of the approach that would prevent practical implementation.

failure_modes.description: Traffic signal optimization requires real-time responsiveness, but gradient descent methods inherently require multiple iterations to converge, making them incompatible with the time constraints of traffic control.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic signals must make decisions in seconds or milliseconds, while gradient descent methods typically require many iterations to approach a solution. The computational complexity alone makes this approach impractical.
